title: Paraneoplastic Limbic Encephalitis Resembling Acute Herpetic Encephalitis
case_prompt:
A 56-year-old man was admitted with a 2-day history of headache, fever up to 38 °C, and acute confusional state. His medical history included hypertension (on perindopril) and heavy smoking (40 cigarettes/day). On examination, he was alert but disoriented (MMSE score 15/30), with no meningeal signs, no focal sensory or motor deficits, and intact cranial nerves. 

Noncontrast head CT was normal. CSF analysis showed 170 cells/mm³ (90% lymphocytes), protein 120 mg/dL, and glucose 71 mg/dL (serum 110 mg/dL). EEG demonstrated diffuse slow activity with paroxysmal slow-wave bursts. Brain MRI showed bilateral contrast-enhancing T2 hyperintense lesions in the medial temporal lobes.

A working diagnosis of acute herpetic encephalitis was made; the patient received intravenous acyclovir and levetiracetam. Routine laboratory assays were unremarkable. Serological tests and CSF PCR for HSV-1/2, VZV, CMV, HHV-6, and Treponema pallidum were negative. On hospital day 3, he developed aphasia, agitation, and two generalized tonic-clonic seizures treated with valproic acid. Six days after admission, he became afebrile but continued to decline cognitively despite ongoing acyclovir therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Herpetic encephalitis was initially suspected for acute onset fever, temporal-lobe involvement, and CSF pleocytosis — “Based on the acute clinical presentation and CSF results, herpetic encephalitis was initially suspected.” It was excluded because “serologic and PCR studies failed to detect any evidence of HSV or other herpesvirus infection and despite treatment with intravenous acyclovir, the patient had a rapidly progressive cognitive decline.”  
2. HHV-6 infection was considered given bilateral temporal-lobe lesions — “Bilateral lesions in medial temporal lobes could be also attributed to HHV-6 infection…” It was excluded because “PCR was negative in our patient and excluded this diagnosis.”  
3. NMDAR encephalitis was considered as part of nonherpetic acute limbic encephalitis — “many of these patients an antibody against NR1/NR2 heteromers of the NMDA receptor was detected; thus, an NMDAR encephalitis was diagnosed.” It was deemed unlikely because “NMDAR encephalitis usually affects young women… About 50% of these patients have an underlying tumor, usually a cystic ovarian teratoma.”  
4. Voltage-gated potassium channel complex antibody–associated LE (mainly LGI1) was considered because it “may present with acute to subacute onset memory loss, confusion, mediotemporal lobe seizures, agitation, and other psychiatric features.” It was excluded by demonstration that “Antibodies against Hu were detected and an extensive screening for underlying neoplasia revealed a large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung. The association of LE with latent neuroendocrine cancer and antibodies to Hu set the diagnosis of anti-Hu PLE.”  
5. Other inflammatory, autoimmune, and neoplastic mimics (e.g., Hashimoto’s encephalopathy, SLE, Sjögren’s syndrome, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, primary CNS angiitis, syphilis, metastases, glioma) were considered and excluded as “Full laboratory assays excluded most of the above mentioned causes, while CSF analysis demonstrated an intense lymphocytic pleocytosis.”
